title: The parting word
hook: when I go from here, let this be my parting word: what I have seen is unsurpassable (Gitanjali 96)
tomorrow: why does a haiku tuck in a word for the season?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: under the trees. Tagore's classroom had no walls, on purpose. Today, the end of the road, and the words Tagore wanted to say when he got there, chosen long before he needed them.
screen: `UNDER THE TREES.` → `THE END OF THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Some people leave a note in their phone for whoever finds it someday. Tagore wrote his goodbye long before he needed it, in Gitanjali's ninety-sixth song: "When I go from hence let this be my parting word, that what I have seen is unsurpassable." Not a regret. Not a warning to the rest of us. A thank-you, written while there was still plenty left to see. His biographers describe him in his last illness, still dictating poems from his bed.
screen: `A NOTE FOR WHOEVER FINDS IT.` → `MY PARTING WORD.` → `NOT A REGRET: A THANK-YOU.`

segments.voice: That parting word picks a side in one of India's long arguments: when you seek God, or when you're leaving, what do you do with the world? One road is renunciation. The sannyasi, the renouncer, gives up home, name and possessions, because attachment binds, and freedom means letting go. Its best case is strong. Tradition says the Buddha left a palace. The Upanishads honor those who leave for the forest. Whatever you cling to, you will lose; loosen your grip first, and you'll be free when it goes. The other road is Tagore's: delight. In Gitanjali's seventy-third song he writes: "Deliverance is not for me in renunciation. I feel the embrace of freedom in a thousand bonds of delight." For him the world is God's own song, and the way out is all the way through: love what you see so fully that leaving becomes thanks. Its best case is strong too. Turning down a gift can look like turning away the giver. Two roads, both walked by serious, loving people for a very long time, and both still walked today. And notice that Tagore's own goodbye keeps a little of each. When he goes, he does let go; he doesn't cling. But he lets go saying that what he has seen could not be surpassed.
screen: `TWO ROADS: LEAVE IT, OR LOVE IT.` · `THE RENOUNCER: LOOSEN YOUR GRIP.` · `TAGORE: BONDS OF DELIGHT.` · `HE LETS GO, GIVING THANKS.` · then, large: `WHAT I HAVE SEEN.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper, and write one line by hand: something you've seen that nothing has topped. Keep it plain: a face, a view, a kitchen late at night. Then sit with the line in front of you for the rest of the two minutes.
The parting word: Gitanjali ninety-six, Tagore's goodbye written in advance, saying that what he has seen of the world is unsurpassable. A farewell that is all thanks.
Your line: what I have seen. Tagore's goodbye was a thank-you to the world. Until next time.

howItsDone: In Hindu life, sannyasa (renunciation) is a recognized path, often taken late in life; Tagore's songs, including Gitanjali's farewell songs, are read and sung at memorials in Bengal.

fork.reveal: that's the renouncer's case, the road of sannyasa. Tagore chose bonds of delight, but he didn't call the other road foolish.
